network.overall_strategy: Prioritize the only route in the supplied literature with experimental continuity to an arginine-specific precursor: the Patel et al. (2015) cyanosulfidic surface branch from acrylonitrile to the arginine alpha-aminonitrile. The graph therefore starts from acrylonitrile as the experimentally defended C3 entry point of that network, then includes both the favored aldehyde-first ordering (34 -> 36 -> 37) and the less favored nitrile-first ordering (34 -> 35 -> 37). Free arginine is reached either by a clearly flagged hydrolysis of intermediate 46 or by a separate late-stage ornithine guanidination route, also flagged as speculative because free-ornithine selectivity in water is unresolved. Disputed direct-arginine claims from HCN polymer hydrolysates are not used as core evidence (Ferris et al., 1973; Ferris et al., 1974).

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.other: ammonia-rich aqueous surface pool or stream; near-neutral to mildly basic

reactions.mechanism: Aza-Michael addition of ammonia to the activated alkene nitrile forms beta-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) use acrylonitrile 33 as the branch-point precursor and explicitly identify beta-aminopropionitrile 34 as the entry to proline/lysine/arginine-related chemistry. This is one of the most secure steps in the arginine-specific network and is straightforward in aqueous ammonia (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: HS-/UV reduction of beta-aminopropionitrile to beta-aminopropionaldehyde

conditions.other: UV-irradiated cyanosulfidic surface setting; H2S/HS- as stoichiometric photoreductant

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox partial reduction of the nitrile followed by hydrolytic release of ammonia yields the aminoaldehyde; sulfur is the formal oxidized sulfur sink.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report HS-/H2S-driven photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile 34 to beta-aminopropionaldehyde 36 in 45% yield. The exact sulfur bookkeeping is not given in the paper, so this node is written as a balanced net with elemental sulfur as the oxidized sulfur product. The surficial sulfide requirement is plausible only in local settings, as discussed by Ranjan et al. (2018), with later related photoredox substitutions by sulfite/ferrocyanide shown by Xu et al. (2018).

reactions.name: Aldehyde-first cyanamide capture

conditions.other: cyanamide present together with the aminoaldehyde in a surface pool; near-neutral pH

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide reacts with the aminoaldehyde to generate a formal guanidino-aldehyde adduct represented here as open-chain intermediate 37.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) note that residual cyanamide reacts very efficiently with beta-aminopropionaldehyde 36 to give adduct 37, and this ordering is the favored branch toward the arginine aminonitrile. Because the supplied review does not resolve the exact solution-state tautomer or cyclized form of 37, the graph uses an open-chain stoichiometric surrogate for the adduct while preserving the reported reaction logic (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Direct guanidinylation of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: cyanamide in aqueous solution; no added activating reagent

reactions.mechanism: Addition of the primary amine to cyanamide gives the guanidinylated nitrile 35.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly report conversion of beta-aminopropionitrile 34 into guanidinylated nitrile 35 with cyanamide, but they describe the step as relatively inefficient and mixture-forming. It is therefore included as a real but less favored alternative to the aldehyde-first branch (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Speculative HS-/UV reduction of guanidino nitrile 35 to aldehyde-level intermediate 37

conditions.other: UV-irradiated sulfide-rich surface pool; written as a balanced net analogous to nitrile-to-aldehyde photoreduction

reactions.mechanism: Formal photoredox partial reduction/hydrolysis of the nitrile gives the same aldehyde-level guanidino intermediate reached by the aldehyde-first route.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. No provided paper isolates this exact one-step conversion from 35 to 37. It is included as a chemically reasonable extrapolation of the Patel et al. (2015) nitrile-to-aldehyde reduction logic, but the literature much more strongly supports the aldehyde-first sequence 34 -> 36 -> 37 than this nitrile-first reduction.

reactions.name: Telescoped reductive homologation from intermediate 37 to cyanohydrin 45

conditions.other: UV-irradiated cyanosulfidic surface chemistry; balanced net corresponds to mol_011 + 2 mol_001 + 2 mol_004 -> mol_012 + mol_002 + 2 mol_008

reactions.mechanism: Sequential HCN addition, sulfide-driven photoreduction, and re-homologation are collapsed into a single balanced net that reaches the C6 cyanohydrin 45.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) describe continued reductive homologation from 37 through thioamide and cyanohydrin intermediates to late intermediate 45, after which ammonia addition gives the arginine alpha-aminonitrile. Because the exact integrated net is not presented in the supplied material, this reaction is deliberately encoded as a telescoped but balanced net requiring two HCN and two H2S equivalents. It is still anchored in the Patel sequence logic and avoids the carbon-deficient lumping criticized in earlier drafts (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Strecker amination to the arginine alpha-aminonitrile

conditions.other: ammonia present in the same cyanosulfidic surface setting; Strecker-type conversion of cyanohydrin 45

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia converts the cyanohydrin 45 to the alpha-aminonitrile 46 with loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) tabulate 45 -> 46 at 90% and identify 46 as the arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor. This is the strongest immediate precursor step in the arginine network, although the authors present full network integration conditionally rather than as a single demonstrated one-pot synthesis (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of the arginine alpha-aminonitrile to arginine

conditions.other: prebiotic pool or geothermal cycling; balanced net corresponds to mol_013 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_015 + mol_002

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid and liberates ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative endgame. Patel et al. (2015) stop at the arginine alpha-aminonitrile and do not report free arginine. Aminonitrile hydrolysis to amino acids is general chemistry, but the review emphasizes that arginine itself can further degrade under harsher hydrolytic conditions, so only mild aqueous hydrolysis under pool or geothermal cycling is defensible. This step is included because a target-level network requires it, not because it is experimentally validated in the supplied arginine literature.

reactions.name: Late guanidination of ornithine with cyanamide

conditions.other: concentrated prebiotic pool or mineral interface; mildly basic conditions likely most favorable; alpha/delta selectivity unresolved

reactions.mechanism: Amidination/guanidination of the side-chain amine of ornithine by cyanamide furnishes the guanidino side chain of arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative but chemically tractable late route. Longo et al. (2020) showed aqueous guanidination of ornithine side chains in a synthetic protein and argued that cyanamide could serve as a primordial guanidinating reagent; Thoma (2023) reports selective ornithine-to-arginine peptide chemistry, but no peer-reviewed demonstration exists for free ornithine + cyanamide in water. Ornithine itself is at least a plausible prebiotic substrate because it was detected in archived Miller spark samples and older cyanide-based experiments, whereas arginine was not (Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011; Longo et al., 2020).

pathways.name: Acrylonitrile to arginine via the favored aldehyde-first branch
pathways.description: Best-supported cyanosulfidic route from the Patel C3 entry point: acrylonitrile is first converted to beta-aminopropionitrile, reduced to the aminoaldehyde, captured by cyanamide, homologated to 45, converted to 46, and then hydrolyzed.

pathways.name: Acrylonitrile to arginine via the less favored nitrile-first branch
pathways.description: Alternative Patel-style route in which cyanamide reacts with beta-aminopropionitrile before nitrile reduction; chemically plausible but explicitly less efficient in the literature.

pathways.name: Beta-aminopropionitrile entry, aldehyde-first continuation
pathways.description: Continuation from beta-aminopropionitrile through aminoaldehyde formation, cyanamide capture, homologation, Strecker amination, and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Beta-aminopropionitrile entry, nitrile-first continuation
pathways.description: Continuation from beta-aminopropionitrile through initial guanidinylation to 35, then reduction, homologation, Strecker amination, and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Aminoaldehyde completion module
pathways.description: Late-stage completion once beta-aminopropionaldehyde is already available in a cyanosulfidic pool.

pathways.name: Intermediate 35 completion module
pathways.description: Late-stage completion once guanidino nitrile 35 has formed; weaker than P5 because the reduction to 37 is not directly demonstrated.

pathways.name: Intermediate 37 to arginine endgame
pathways.description: The compact late Patel branch: reductive homologation of 37 to 45, Strecker amination to 46, then hydrolysis to arginine.

pathways.name: Intermediate 45 to arginine completion
pathways.description: Shortest literature-grounded precursor route that still includes the experimentally strong 45 -> 46 step before hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Aminonitrile hydrolysis endgame
pathways.description: Minimal target-forming step from the Patel arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor 46 to free arginine; chemically plausible but not experimentally demonstrated in the supplied prebiotic literature.

pathways.name: Late ornithine guanidination route
pathways.description: Alternative late-stage pathway in which preformed ornithine is converted directly to arginine by cyanamide; included because the endgame is chemically reasonable, but it remains unverified for free ornithine in water.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strongest full route and best aligned with the favored Patel aldehyde-first branch. rxn_001-rxn_003 are chemically credible under cyanosulfidic surface conditions. The main weaknesses are rxn_006, which is a compressed homologation and should consume 2 HCN and 2 H2S, and rxn_008, which should consume 2 H2O and is not demonstrated prebiotically for arginine. The Surface to Biochemical handoff is also not physically justified.
suggestions: Correct rxn_006 stoichiometry or split it into literature-supported substeps.
Correct rxn_008 to use 2 H2O and specify a plausible nonbiological hydrolysis setting.
Add Cu(I), UV, phosphate, and a transport scenario to strengthen environmental realism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route reaches the same target class but is notably weaker than P1. Direct cyanamide capture at rxn_004 is known to be inefficient, rxn_005 is explicitly speculative because reduction of intermediate 35 to 37 was not shown in the cited literature, and rxn_006 and rxn_008 also need stoichiometric correction: 2 HCN + 2 H2S in rxn_006 and 2 H2O in rxn_008. Free arginine remains proposed rather than experimentally established.
suggestions: Prefer the aldehyde-first ordering unless experimental support for 35 to 37 is added.
Correct the stoichiometry of rxn_006 and rxn_008.
Provide explicit conditions showing that the guanidino group survives the reductive homologation sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Coherent continuation of the best-supported Patel branch once beta-aminopropionitrile is granted. The main issues are the telescoped rxn_006 stoichiometry, which needs 2 HCN and 2 H2S, the lack of explicit Cu(I), UV, and phosphate conditions, and the unverified hydrolysis in rxn_008, which needs 2 H2O and remains speculative for arginine.
suggestions: Correct or decompose rxn_006 into the literature-supported homologation sequence.
Relabel the final setting as a plausible aqueous hydrolysis environment rather than a generic biochemical one.
Keep the route explicitly capped at the arginine alpha-aminonitrile unless hydrolysis evidence is supplied.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This continuation inherits the weak points of the nitrile-first ordering. rxn_005 is the main evidence gap, rxn_006 is compressed and mis-specified stoichiometrically, and rxn_008 is an unverified hydrolysis to free arginine. It is a plausible proposal, but not a well-supported literature path.
suggestions: Add direct experimental support for 35 to 37 or demote this branch further.
Correct rxn_006 to include 2 HCN and 2 H2S.
Specify prebiotically credible hydrolysis conditions for rxn_008 or stop at the aminonitrile.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: As a module from the aminoaldehyde, this is chemically coherent and literature-aligned through rxn_007. Confidence drops at rxn_006 because the compressed homologation needs 2 HCN and 2 H2S and hides intermediate steps, and at rxn_008 because hydrolysis to arginine is not demonstrated prebiotically and should use 2 H2O.
suggestions: Expand rxn_006 into named intermediate steps from the Patel sequence.
Correct rxn_008 stoichiometry and provide realistic hydrolysis conditions.
State the UV, sulfide, and catalyst assumptions explicitly for the surface stage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This module is weakened by the speculative 35 to 37 reduction in rxn_005, then carries the same rxn_006 stoichiometric issue and the same uncertain final hydrolysis. It is a reasonable hypothesis but not a defended completion sequence.
suggestions: Validate rxn_005 experimentally or remove this module as a serious route.
Correct rxn_006 stoichiometry and make the hidden intermediates explicit.
Treat rxn_008 as unresolved unless direct hydrolysis data are available.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The endgame from intermediate 37 is plausible up to the arginine alpha-aminonitrile, especially via rxn_007. However, rxn_006 should be written with 2 HCN and 2 H2S or decomposed into substeps, and rxn_008 remains the unresolved step for actual free arginine formation.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_006 with the correct stoichiometry or split it into the Patel substeps.
Provide a specific aqueous setting for hydrolysis rather than a generic biochemical environment.
If no hydrolysis evidence is available, designate the aminonitrile as the terminal verified product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the cleanest literature-supported short endgame to the arginine alpha-aminonitrile because rxn_007 is strong. The pathway still does not convincingly close to free arginine: rxn_008 needs 2 H2O stoichiometrically, lacks a defended prebiotic environment, and is not experimentally shown for this substrate.
suggestions: Correct rxn_008 to consume 2 H2O.
Specify hydrolysis conditions that preserve the guanidino group and are prebiotically credible.
Consider stopping the validated route at the aminonitrile and marking arginine formation as hypothetical.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: As a one-step hydrolysis endgame, this nominally gives the target but is weak evidence for synthesis of free arginine. The reaction should consume 2 H2O, and no realistic prebiotic setting or yield is provided; the cited literature stops at the aminonitrile.
suggestions: Correct the stoichiometry to mol_013 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_015 + mol_002.
Specify temperature, pH, and mineral or catalytic context for hydrolysis.
Add evidence that arginine survives the chosen hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This direct ornithine guanidination route is chemically conceivable and balanced, but the evidence gap is large. Published prebiotic chemistry does not establish efficient, selective conversion of free ornithine to arginine with cyanamide in water, and competing alpha versus delta guanidination and ornithine side reactions are not addressed. The Biochemical environment label is too vague to count as a defended prebiotic setting.
suggestions: Provide direct experimental precedent for free-ornithine guanidination by cyanamide under plausible conditions.
Specify pH, temperature, concentration, and any mineral or drying context to justify the environment.
If retained, either connect ornithine to the rest of the network or clearly mark this as an auxiliary hypothesis.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is strong: 15 molecules and 9 reactions form a connected graph, IDs are consistent, and the supplied RDKit check reports 0 unbalanced reactions. Literature alignment is also strong because the network prioritizes the Patel cyanosulfidic arginine-precursor branch and treats free arginine formation as unresolved. The main limitations are chemical and environmental rather than topological: rxn_005 is speculative; rxn_006 is a compressed homologation and should be corrected to mol_011 + 2 mol_001 + 2 mol_004 -> mol_012 + mol_002 + 2 mol_008; rxn_008 should be mol_013 + 2 mol_005 -> mol_015 + mol_002 and remains experimentally unverified for prebiotic arginine; and rxn_009 lacks evidence for efficient, selective free-ornithine guanidination by cyanamide in water. Surface cyanosulfidic steps would be more convincing with explicit Cu(I), UV, phosphate, and a justified post-surface hydrolysis setting. Overall, the network credibly reaches the arginine alpha-aminonitrile but only proposes, rather than demonstrates, synthesis of free arginine, so it is not approved at the >=0.9 network threshold.
